activities.anchor: packing infinite thoughts into a finite toolbox
activities.caption: call the count — languages alive
activities.name: hlOctopusEstimate

config.prompt: Roughly how many languages are alive in the world today?
config.why: Just over 7,000 — and you can build a sentence nobody in history has ever uttered ('the octopus filed a complaint about the lift music') that any adult speaker parses instantly. Speaking is running a system, not consulting a phrasebook.
config.context: About half of them have fewer than ~7,000 speakers — the family section below.

activities.anchor: coordinated breath, vocal cords, tongue and lips
activities.caption: pair each piece of the machinery with its role
activities.name: hlSkillsMatch

config.prompt: The most complex behaviour on the planet — pair the piece with its role:

pairs.left: producing language in real time, at up to several words per second
pairs.right: the expressive skills — with almost no conscious effort

pairs.left: negotiating who owes whom an apology
pairs.right: reaching other minds — what the machinery is for

config.why: Language is how we draw conclusions together, set goals and hand down everything a community knows; strip it away and human intelligence as we know it would not survive.

activities.anchor: Three facts show how deep the system runs
activities.caption: file each observation under the property it shows
activities.name: hlFactsBuckets

config.prompt: File each observation under the property it shows:

items.label: a five-year-old commands English word order flawlessly but cannot state the rule
every language orders its sentence elements by discoverable universals
the patterns are statistical and systematic, not loose habits
Humboldt's phrase: making 'infinite use of finite means'
you 'just know' it without ever being taught

config.why: Implicit: the knowledge outruns any statement of it. Law-governed: universals, not habits. Creative: a finite toolbox, an infinite range.

activities.anchor: Think of phonemes as the atoms of speech
activities.caption: find the line the spelling would have to obey
activities.name: hlPhonSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is false — click it:
lines: The phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that can change meaning.
English runs on about 44 phonemes squeezed into 26 letters.
Letters and phonemes map one-to-one in English spelling.
config.correction: 26 letters carry about 44 phonemes — the mismatch is the spelling chaos.
config.why: Individually featureless, decisive in combination: the atoms of speech never lined up cleanly with the alphabet.

activities.anchor: Phoneme inventories vary enormously across languages
activities.caption: true or false — trained to hear
activities.name: hlPhonJudge

statements.s: Hawaiian manages with 13 sounds in total.
statements.why: English runs about 24 consonants and 20 vowels — inventories vary enormously.

statements.s: Some Khoisan languages deploy dozens of click consonants.
statements.why: The same universal design, wildly different sound stock.

statements.s: The breathy difference between English 'p' in 'pin' and 'spin' is meaningful in Hindi but invisible to most English-speaking adults.
statements.why: Which differences count is language-specific — adults literally struggle to hear it.

statements.s: Your phoneme inventory is just what you can say.
statements.why: It is what you have been trained to hear — the listening side runs the inventory.

activities.anchor: Languages differ wildly in how much work morphemes do
activities.caption: one Turkish word, whole clause
activities.name: hlTurkishCloze

config.text: English strings words separately ('will not have been going'); Turkish packs the whole clause into one word: %%0%% — 'from your houses'.
config.hint: Build it piece by piece: ev-ler-iniz-den = house-plural-your-from.
config.why: English is fairly analytic — it strings separate words; Latin, Turkish or Swahili are synthetic and pack entire clauses into one unit.

activities.caption: unstack the house that Jack built
activities.name: hlNestOrder

config.prompt: Recursion in action — order the stack from the outermost sentence down:
items: The cat — the whole sentence is about it
that sat in the house that Jack built
config.why: Rules that apply to their own output: nothing in principle stops the loop, which is how a finite rulebook generates infinite sentences — and all three word orders (SVO, SOV, VSO) build the same stack with the same underlying logic.

activities.anchor: which is why irony, politeness and hinting survive translation only imperfectly
activities.caption: answer the flatmate — literally or pragmatically
activities.name: hlSaltBranch

config.root: Pragmatics: meaning in context. Two utterances, two chances to take them literally.

start.text: Your flatmate, staring at the open window: 'It's cold in here.' What do you do?

choices.label: Report the thermostat reading
choices.feedback: Technically responsive — and completely beside the point.

choices.label: Get up and close the window
choices.feedback: You just computed a request that never said 'close it'. The situation completed the meaning.

literal.text: Now the classic: 'Can you pass the salt?' — a question about your physical ability?

choices.label: Demonstrate the ability by lifting the shaker
choices.feedback: Everyone still expected the salt in their hand.

choices.label: Pass the salt
choices.feedback: Indirect speech acts: processed without effort, everywhere.

show.text: You answered the question literally — the words said one thing, the situation said another.

done.text: Indirect requests, digs and sarcasm are computed from conventions every language equips its speakers with.

config.why: The words say one thing; the situation completes the meaning — the layer above semantics runs on shared conventions.
